title: He called down fire…
paragraphs: …and then asked God to take his life.
How does a man go from victory to wanting to disappear?

How do you stand on a mountain one day—
and collapse under a tree the next?
Because this isn’t just Elijah’s story.

This is what failure feels like after the applause fades.
This is what shame whispers when the crowd goes home.
This is what happens when your strength runs out—and your soul has nothing left to hide behind.
Elijah just defeated the prophets of Baal.

Fire fell.
The people shouted.
God proved Himself.
And yet—just one threat from Jezebel…

Fear took over.
Exhaustion set in.
Isolation wrapped around his mind like a noose.
And suddenly the prophet who stood fearless before a nation…
Listen carefully to his breaking point:

“But he himself went a day’s journey into the wilderness and came and sat down under a broom tree. And he asked that he might die, saying, ‘It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life, for I am no better than my fathers.’” — 1 Kings 19:4
That line hits different when you’ve been there.
Shame doesn’t just say, “You did wrong.”

It rewrites your identity.
It edits your worth.
It convinces you that your story has peaked—and now it’s only decline from here.
And maybe that’s where you are right now.

You prayed.
You believed.
You fought.
But something didn’t turn out the way you expected.
Now you’re sitting under your own “broom tree”—

“You’re not enough.”
“You failed again.”
“God is done with you.”
Because what happens next in Elijah’s story will either confront your shame…
But not the way you expect.

No thunder.
No rebuke.
No disappointment.
“And he lay down and slept under a broom tree. And behold, an angel touched him and said to him, ‘Arise and eat.’” — 1 Kings 19:5

“And he arose and ate and drank and lay down again. And the angel of the LORD came again a second time and touched him and said, ‘Arise and eat, for the journey is too great for you.’” — 1 Kings 19:6–7
“The journey is too great for you.”
God wasn’t surprised by Elijah’s breaking point.
Some of you are drowning in shame because you think your weakness disqualifies you.
But God already knows your limits.
He’s not shocked by your exhaustion.
He’s not offended by your tears.
He’s not pacing heaven saying, “I expected more from you.”
He’s saying, “I know this is heavy. Let Me sustain you.”
But here’s where the tension deepens.
“I, even I only, am left, and they seek my life, to take it away.” — 1 Kings 19:10

It convinces you that no one understands.
That no one else struggles like you.
That you are uniquely broken.
But God answers that lie directly:
“Yet I will leave seven thousand in Israel, all the knees that have not bowed to Baal…” — 1 Kings 19:18
Elijah thought he was the last.
Let me speak this into your life:
You are not as alone as your thoughts make you feel.
But the story doesn’t stop with Elijah.
Because Elijah’s breakdown points to something deeper—
A separation from God that no amount of effort, discipline, or spiritual activity can fix.
And here’s the truth we don’t like to admit:
Sometimes our greatest exhaustion doesn’t come from doing too little…
…but from trying to carry what we were never meant to carry.
We try to outrun our own brokenness.
Because the journey is too great for us.
That’s where the Gospel breaks in.
Because while Elijah sat under a tree asking to die—
Jesus went to a tree to give life.
“He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness.” — 1 Peter 2:24
Elijah said, “It is enough” in despair.
Where Elijah felt like a failure—
Jesus fulfilled what we never could.
Where we collapse under the weight of sin—
Where shame tells you, “You’re not enough”—
You are more broken than you admit.
But more loved than you can imagine.
And salvation is not found in trying harder—
but in surrendering fully to Jesus Christ.
“For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God.” — Ephesians 2:8
but trusting Him with your life.
What are you carrying right now that Jesus already paid for?
What lie have you believed so long that it feels like truth?
What “broom tree” have you been sitting under, convincing yourself that your story is over?
God did not finish Elijah under that tree.
And He’s not finishing you there either.
But you cannot stay where shame wants to keep you.
Bring your failure into the light.
Lay your shame at the cross.
And receive what Jesus already finished.
Because the same God who fed Elijah in his lowest moment…
“Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28
And if this stirred something deep in your spirit…
